what_it_means_heading: What ceiling fan installation actually involves
what_it_means_paragraphs: Ceiling fan installation is more than hanging a fan on a hook. A ceiling fan weighs 15 to 50 pounds and spins for years, so it has to mount to a UL-listed fan-rated electrical box anchored to the framing — not the thin pancake box that holds a light fixture, and never just the drywall. Most of the wobbling, rattling, and dropped-fan calls we get trace back to one thing: a fan hung on a box that was never rated to carry a moving load. Getting the box right is the whole job.

There are three common versions of the work. Swapping an old fan for a new one where a fan already hangs is the quick version — assuming the existing box is fan-rated. Replacing a light fixture with a fan means upgrading the box and often adding a switch leg so you can control the fan and light separately. Putting a fan where there's no fixture at all — a bedroom or living room that never had one — means running new wiring, cutting in a box, and adding a switch, which is the most involved version. We tell you which one you're looking at before we quote it.

{owner_name} is a {license_state}-licensed Master Electrician — the highest electrician tier the state issues — serving {city_name} and the surrounding area. The approach is straightforward: confirm the box and framing can carry the load, mount it dead level, wire the fan and light to the right switches, and balance the blades so it runs quiet at every speed. If your ceiling is vaulted, two stories up, or you want a smart or remote-controlled fan, that's normal work for us, not a reason to turn the job down.

problems_intro_template: Here are the calls {owner_first_name} gets most often from {city_name} homeowners. If your situation matches one of these, you're in the right place.

problem_cards.title: Replacing a light fixture with a ceiling fan
problem_cards.body: The most common request — and the one most likely to be done wrong by a handyman. The existing light box almost never carries a fan. We swap it for a UL-listed fan-rated box braced to the joists, run the extra switch leg if you want separate fan and light control, and mount the fan level.

problem_cards.title: Adding a fan to a room that never had one
problem_cards.body: No existing fixture means new work: fishing wire through the ceiling, cutting in a fan-rated box, and adding a wall switch. It's the most involved version of the job, but it's routine for us. We'll tell you on-site whether your ceiling and attic access make it a clean run or a more involved one.

problem_cards.title: Fan wobbles, rattles, or drops
problem_cards.body: A wobbling fan is almost always a mounting problem — a non-fan-rated box, loose blades, or a fan never balanced after install. A fan that's working loose is a safety issue. We re-mount it to a proper rated box, balance the blades, and make sure it runs quiet at high speed, not just low.

problem_cards.title: Vaulted, sloped, or two-story ceilings
problem_cards.body: High and angled ceilings need a sloped-ceiling adapter, a downrod sized to bring the fan to the right height, and the right ladder or scaffold to reach it safely. We carry downrods and slope kits and have the equipment to work two stories up — this is normal work, not an upcharge surprise.

problem_cards.title: Old fan swap for a new one
problem_cards.body: If a fan already hangs and the box is fan-rated, swapping in a new fan is quick. We confirm the existing box and wiring are sound, install your new fan or one we supply, and haul the old one away. If the existing box turns out not to be rated, we tell you before we touch it.

problem_cards.title: Outdoor and covered-patio fans
problem_cards.body: Porches, patios, and screened rooms need a fan rated for damp or wet locations and a box and wiring to match. A standard indoor fan installed outside will fail. We install the correct wet- or damp-rated fan and weatherproof the connection.

problem_cards.title: Smart, remote, and app-controlled fans
problem_cards.body: Modern fans add a remote, a wall control, or Wi-Fi and app control. The wiring behind them isn't always plug-and-play — some need a separate hot for the receiver, some replace the wall switch entirely. We wire it so the remote, the wall switch, and the app all behave the way you expect.

problem_cards.title: Fan and light controlled separately
problem_cards.body: If you want the light on while the fan is off, or to dim the light without slowing the fan, you need the right switch setup — often a dual switch or a fan/light control. We add the switch leg and install the control so each works on its own.

process_intro_template: When you call {phone_display} or request a quote online, here's what happens.

process_steps.title: A real conversation about the job
process_steps.body: We pick up. You tell us the room, the ceiling height, and whether there's a fan or fixture there now. We ask whether you're supplying the fan or want us to, and whether you want separate fan-and-light control. That tells us which version of the job it is and what to bring.

process_steps.title: On-site check and written estimate
process_steps.body: We look at the existing box, the framing, the switch, and the ceiling. You get a written estimate before any work starts — box upgrade if needed, fan install, any new wiring or switch, and haul-away of the old fan. No surprise charges on the work day.

process_steps.title: The right fan-rated box and brace
process_steps.body: If the existing box isn't fan-rated, this is the step that matters most. We install a UL-listed fan-rated box anchored to the framing — the part that keeps your fan on the ceiling for the next fifteen years. We carry these on the truck so it doesn't become a second trip.

process_steps.title: Mount, wire, and level
process_steps.body: We mount the fan dead level, size the downrod to the ceiling height, and wire the fan and light to the correct switches. Sloped ceiling, two stories up, outdoor-rated — we have the adapters and the equipment to do it right.

process_steps.title: Balance and test every speed
process_steps.body: A new fan isn't done until it runs quiet. We balance the blades, test low, medium, and high, check the remote and wall control, and confirm the light and fan behave independently if that's what you asked for. Then we clean up and haul the old fan away.

faq_items.question: Can you install a ceiling fan where there's only a light fixture now?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes — it's one of our most common jobs. The catch is the box: the box holding your light fixture almost never carries the weight and motion of a fan, so we swap it for a UL-listed fan-rated box braced to the framing. If you want to control the fan and light separately, we add a switch leg so each works on its own. We confirm what your ceiling needs on-site and give you the written estimate before any work starts. Call {phone_display} and tell us the room and ceiling height.

faq_items.question: Why does my ceiling fan wobble, and can you fix it?
faq_items.answer_html: Almost always, a wobbling fan is a mounting problem, not a fan problem. The usual cause is a box that was never fan-rated — a fan hung on a light box or directly on drywall will wobble and, over time, work loose, which is a safety issue. The other causes are unbalanced or warped blades and a loose downrod. We re-mount the fan to a proper fan-rated box anchored to framing, balance the blades, and tighten everything down so it runs quiet at high speed, not just on low. If the fan itself is failing, we'll tell you that too.

faq_items.question: Can you install a fan on a vaulted or two-story ceiling?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes. Sloped and high ceilings are routine for us. A vaulted ceiling needs a sloped-ceiling adapter so the fan hangs level instead of at an angle, and a downrod sized to bring the fan down to the right height for airflow. A two-story foyer or great room needs the right ladder or scaffold to reach it safely — which we have. We carry downrods and slope kits on the truck, so a high or angled ceiling doesn't turn into a return trip. Tell us the ceiling height when you call and we'll come prepared.

faq_items.question: How long does ceiling fan installation take?
faq_items.answer_html: A straight swap, where a fan-rated box already exists, usually takes under an hour. Replacing a light fixture with a fan, including the box upgrade and any switch work, typically runs one to two hours. Adding a fan to a room with no existing fixture takes longer because it involves running new wiring and cutting in a box and switch — often a half-day depending on attic access and the wiring run. We give you a realistic time estimate along with the price before we start, so you know what to expect.

faq_items.question: Can you set up the fan and light to work separately?
faq_items.answer_html: Yes. If you want the light on while the fan is off, the fan running without the light, or the ability to dim the light without slowing the fan, you need the right switch setup — usually a dual switch or a dedicated fan/light control at the wall. We add the switch leg and install the control so each one operates independently. Many modern fans also include a remote; we make sure the remote, the wall control, and the fan all behave consistently so you're not fighting the controls. Tell us how you want to control it and we'll wire it that way.

faq_items.question: Is it safe to install a ceiling fan myself?
faq_items.answer_html: The risk isn't the wiring so much as the mount. A ceiling fan weighs 15 to 50 pounds and spins for years, so it has to hang from a UL-listed fan-rated box anchored to the framing. The most common DIY mistake is hanging a fan on the existing light box or on the drywall — it holds at first, then works loose, wobbles, and in the worst case comes down. There's also the wiring side: getting the fan and light on the correct switches, and not overloading a circuit. A licensed electrician gets the box, the wiring, and the balance right the first time. Call {phone_display} if you'd rather not gamble on the mount.
